title: Hot or Cold? Radial Redistribution of Stars in FIRE Simulations of Milky Way-Mass Galaxies and the Asymmetry of Inward versus Outward Migrators
comment: 25 pages, submitted to The Open Journal of Astrophysics
summary: Stars can radially redistribute (migrate) within galactic disks. The degree to which this occurs as dynamically `cold' (preserves orbital eccentricity) or `hot' (increases eccentricity) remains debated. Many models presume that radial redistribution occurs primarily via cold torquing, resulting in changes in angular momentum without dynamical heating. We test the net dynamical heating associated with redistribution over stellar lifetimes using the FIRE cosmological zoom-in simulations of 12 Milky Way-mass galaxies. We select star particles today that underwent significant changes in orbital angular momentum, j_phi, since birth. We investigate net changes in their orbital eccentricity, e, and we quantify the `cold-torqued' fraction of star particles with |Delta j_phi/j_phi,birth| > 0.2 that preserved eccentricity (|Delta e| < 0.1) since birth. The direction of radial redistribution is most critical: outward-migrating stars experienced smaller net changes in eccentricity, whereas inward-migrating stars almost always heat since birth. For stars born on near-circular orbits (e_birth < 0.2), the cold-torqued fraction decreases rapidly with age today and is generally < 50% at ages >~2 Gyr. Stars born on moderately eccentric orbits (e_birth ~ 0.4) are the most likely to preserve their birth eccentricity. However, the cold-torqued fraction is higher in earlier-forming and/or dynamically-colder disks. Significantly, we identify a population of stars that dynamically `cooled', decreasing in eccentricity since birth: this is the primary way that stars end up on near-circular orbits today. Overall, a star's migration direction, its e_birth, and its age primarily determine whether it was dynamically heated, cooled, or unchanged. In general, radial redistribution in FIRE is typically not cold between birth and today.

AI.tldr: Using FIRE cosmological simulations of 12 Milky Way-mass galaxies, the authors test whether stellar radial redistribution in galactic disks is dynamically "cold" (preserving orbital eccentricity) or "hot" (increasing eccentricity). They find that outward-migrating stars experience smaller eccentricity changes, inward-migrating stars almost always heat up, and the cold-torqued fraction is generally <50% for stars older than ~2 Gyr. A population of stars that dynamically "cool" (decrease eccentricity) is identified. Overall, radial redistribution is typically not cold between birth and present day.
AI.motivation: To resolve the debate over whether radial migration of stars in galactic disks occurs predominantly via cold torquing (preserving orbital eccentricity) or hot processes (increasing eccentricity), by testing the net dynamical heating associated with radial redistribution over stellar lifetimes.
AI.method: Analyzed FIRE cosmological zoom-in simulations of 12 Milky Way-mass galaxies. Selected star particles with significant changes in orbital angular momentum (|Δj_phi/j_phi,birth| > 0.2) and quantified the cold-torqued fraction as those preserving eccentricity (|Δe| < 0.1) since birth. Examined dependencies on migration direction, birth eccentricity, age, and disk formation history.
AI.result: Outward-migrating stars experience smaller eccentricity changes than inward-migrating stars, which almost always heat. Cold-torqued fraction is generally <50% for stars older than ~2 Gyr and decreases with age. Stars born on moderately eccentric orbits (e_birth ~ 0.4) are most likely to preserve eccentricity. A population of dynamically "cooled" stars exists. Cold-torqued fraction is higher in earlier-forming and dynamically-colder disks.
AI.conclusion: Radial redistribution in FIRE simulations is typically not cold between birth and today. Migration direction, birth eccentricity, and age are the primary determinants of whether a star is dynamically heated, cooled, or unchanged.

title: Little Red Dots at z~2 in EIGER reveal a gentle decline with respect to their peak number density at z~5
comment: Main text 13 pages, 11 figures. Submitted to A&A. Comments welcome
summary: We report the discovery of a sample of little red dots (LRDs) at $z \approx 2$ identified from deep JWST/NIRCam imaging and wide-field slitless spectroscopy over $140$ arcmin$^2$ from the EIGER survey. With an improved blind broad-line identification algorithm, we select 19 sources at spectroscopic redshifts $z = 1.55-3.18$ identified via rest-frame near-infrared lines (Paschen-$β$, HeI+Pa$γ$ and OI). Based on a range of spectro-photometric criteria, we classify five of these sources as LRDs and the other 14 as classical active galactic nuclei (AGNs). This classification is corroborated by some X-ray detections among the AGNs. Classical AGNs dominate the number counts above optical luminosities M$_{5100}<-22.5$, whereas the LRD fraction among broad-line sources reaches 100 % at M$_{5100}\approx-20$. The LRDs span the range in Balmer break strengths seen in the higher redshift populations. Blue-shifted HeI absorption is detected in the two reddest sources. The HeI/Pa$γ$ ratio cleanly separates LRDs from classical AGNs and seems to anti-correlate with Balmer break strength, likely tracing HeI self-absorption at higher gas column densities. Our LRD sample has a similar optical luminosity range as their high-redshift counterparts, corresponding to black hole masses of $\sim10^{6}$ M$_{\odot}$ at the Eddington luminosity. We measure LRD number densities of $\approx 7\times10^{-6}$ cMpc$^{-3}$ at $z = 1.9-2.5$, which indicates that LRDs represent $\lesssim 3$ % of the AGN population at these epochs. Our results confirm the previously reported decline in the LRD number density with respect to $z \approx 5$ based on photometric surveys, although we find the decline to be more gentle than earlier emphasized.

AI.tldr: Using EIGER JWST/NIRCam data over 140 arcmin², the authors identify 19 broad-line sources at z≈2 (via Paβ, HeI+Paγ, OI). Five are classified as little red dots (LRDs) and 14 as classical AGNs. LRDs dominate at low optical luminosity (M₅₁₀₀≈-20) with black hole masses ~10⁶ M☉ at Eddington limit, while their number density ~7×10⁻⁶ cMpc⁻³ (z=1.9-2.5) is ≤3% of the AGN population, confirming a decline from z≈5.
AI.motivation: To identify and characterize little red dots (LRDs) at lower redshifts (z≈2) using deep JWST/NIRCam imaging and slitless spectroscopy from the EIGER survey, and to compare their properties and number densities with higher-redshift LRD populations.
AI.method: Blind broad-line identification algorithm applied to JWST/NIRCam wide-field slitless spectroscopy over 140 arcmin². Selection of 19 sources at spectroscopic redshifts z=1.55-3.18 via rest-frame near-infrared lines (Paβ, HeI+Paγ, OI). Classification into LRDs and classical AGNs based on spectro-photometric criteria, with X-ray detections used as corroboration. HeI/Paγ ratio and Balmer break strengths analyzed.
AI.result: Five LRDs and 14 classical AGNs identified. Classical AGNs dominate at M₅₁₀₀<-22.5, while LRDs reach 100% of broad-line sources at M₅₁₀₀≈-20. LRDs span the Balmer break range seen at higher z. Blue-shifted HeI absorption found in the two reddest sources. HeI/Paγ ratio cleanly separates LRDs from classical AGNs and anti-correlates with Balmer break. LRD number density ≈7×10⁻⁶ cMpc⁻³ at z=1.9-2.5, representing ≤3% of the AGN population. Confirms a more gentle decline from z≈5 than previously emphasized.
AI.conclusion: The study confirms the existence of LRDs at z≈2 with properties similar to their higher-redshift counterparts, shows that LRDs are a low-luminosity subpopulation of AGNs at these epochs, and provides spectroscopic evidence for a more gradual decline in LRD number density from z≈5 than inferred from photometric surveys alone.

title: The multiwavelength structure of post-starburst galaxies at 0.5 < z < 3 with JWST PRIMER: compact morphologies and residual disturbances
comment: 22 pages, 18 figures, Published in MNRAS
summary: We investigate the multi-wavelength structure of recently quenched post-starburst (PSB) galaxies at 0.5 < z < 3, using photometrically selected samples from the Ultra Deep Survey (UDS). Leveraging deep eight-band JWST/NIRCam imaging from the PRIMER programme, we analyze ~120 PSBs across the rest-frame optical-to-near-infrared, and compare with a reference sample of ~3000 passive and star-forming galaxies. Structural parameters (effective radius Re and Sersic index n) are derived independently in each waveband, and reveal that PSBs exhibit minimal structural variation with wavelength, indicating negligible stellar population age gradients or internal dust obscuration. We confirm that PSBs follow the established redshift-mass trends: at z > 1, massive PSBs (M* > 10^10 Msun) are compact spheroids resembling massive passive galaxies, albeit significantly more compact, whereas at 0.5 < z < 1, PSBs are typically low-mass (M* < 10^10 Msun) compact, disc-dominated systems akin to low-mass passive discs. Furthermore, for the first time, we systematically quantify disturbance indicators (residual flux fraction RFF, asymmetry, residual asymmetry) across a large PSB sample. At all masses, PSBs exhibit low RFF and asymmetry values comparable to passive systems and consistent with smooth, largely undisturbed morphologies. However, at z > 1, massive PSBs (M* > 10^10.25 Msun) show enhanced residual asymmetry relative to the passive population, indicating a previously unrecognized level of structural disturbance masked beneath a smooth stellar distribution. These results suggest that, while structural transformation is largely complete by the PSB phase, residual disturbances persist at high redshift, supporting a scenario in which rapid quenching proceeds via two distinct pathways: highly disruptive events (e.g. major mergers) at high z and high mass, and comparatively gentle processes at later times.

AI.tldr: This study analyzes ~120 post-starburst (PSB) galaxies at 0.5<z<3 using JWST/NIRCam data from PRIMER/UDS. PSBs show minimal structural variation with wavelength (no age gradients or dust obscuration). High-z massive PSBs are compact spheroids with enhanced residual asymmetry not seen in passive galaxies, while low-z PSBs are low-mass compact discs. Results suggest two quenching pathways: disruptive major mergers at high-z/mass, and gentler processes at later times.
AI.motivation: To characterize the multi-wavelength structure of post-starburst galaxies across a broad redshift range (0.5<z<3) and understand the evolutionary pathways leading to rapid quenching, particularly whether structural transformation is complete by the PSB phase.
AI.method: Photometrically selected PSB samples from UDS; deep eight-band JWST/NIRCam imaging from PRIMER; structural parameters (Re, Sersic n) derived independently per waveband; disturbance indicators (RFF, asymmetry, residual asymmetry) systematically quantified across the sample.
AI.result: PSBs show negligible wavelength-dependent structural variation. At z>1, massive PSBs are compact spheroids; at 0.5<z<1, low-mass PSBs are compact discs. PSBs generally show low disturbance comparable to passive galaxies, but massive PSBs at z>1 exhibit enhanced residual asymmetry indicating hidden structural disturbances.
AI.conclusion: Structural transformation is largely complete by the PSB phase, but residual disturbances persist at high redshift. Supports a scenario with two rapid quenching pathways: highly disruptive events (major mergers) at high z/mass, and gentler processes at lower redshifts.

title: The Fleeting Laboratory: An Experimental Guide for Total Solar Eclipses
summary: Since times immemorial, total solar eclipses have inspired awe and wonder. In the modern scientific era they have transformed into exclusive natural laboratories, offering fleeting but invaluable opportunities to study the Sun's faint outer atmosphere otherwise obscured by the intense glare of the photosphere. This unique vantage point has enabled revolutionary discoveries, from the identification of the element Helium and the first empirical validation of Einstein's General Relativity, to deciphering the corona's surprisingly high temperature. This legacy of discovery continues. Today, ground-based eclipse experiments provide crucial data that complements and calibrates our space-based solar observatories, and offer high-resolution capabilities in the spatial, temporal as well as spectral domains. This chapter serves as a comprehensive guide detailing how to leverage modern observing equipments, detectors, and advanced computational techniques in image and data processing to conduct meaningful scientific investigations, bridging the gap between historical precedent and cutting-edge research.

AI.tldr: Total solar eclipses serve as exclusive natural laboratories for studying the Sun's faint corona, enabling historic discoveries (Helium, General Relativity, coronal heating). Modern ground-based eclipse experiments complement space-based observatories with high-resolution data. This chapter provides a comprehensive guide on using modern equipment, detectors, and computational techniques to conduct meaningful scientific investigations.
AI.motivation: Total solar eclipses provide unique opportunities to study the Sun's faint outer atmosphere (corona), which is otherwise obscured by the photosphere's glare, enabling observations impossible to replicate with current technology.
AI.method: Leveraging modern observing equipment, detectors, and advanced computational techniques in image and data processing for ground-based eclipse experiments.
AI.result: Ground-based eclipse experiments provide crucial data that complements and calibrates space-based solar observatories, offering high-resolution capabilities across spatial, temporal, and spectral domains.
AI.conclusion: This chapter bridges historical precedent and cutting-edge research by providing a comprehensive guide for conducting meaningful scientific investigations during total solar eclipses using modern instrumentation and computational methods.

title: Search for Quasar Pairs with ${\it Gaia}$ Astrometric Data. III. Discovery of 9 dual and projected quasars
comment: 14 pages, 6 figures, 2 tables. Submitted to A&A, comments welcome!
summary: We report the low-resolution long-slit spectroscopic observations and confirmations of 11 quasar pair candidates, which are selected from the MGQPC catalog presented in the first paper of our series work (hereafter, Paper-I) and the early version of this catalog. The spectroscopic follow-up was carried out with 5 spectrographs equipped on 3 telescopes, and the major discoveries include 6 dual quasars and 3 projected quasars. One of the dual quasars has a high redshift of $\sim$ 3.1. The LQ hypothesis of 3 dual quasars cannot be completely ruled out. We investigated the reason why previous spectroscopic surveys missed several new quasars. We discussed a projected quasar with a wide-separation lensing configuration, as well as two quasar-star projections that mimic the configuration of lensed quasars. The photometric redshifts for the 11 observed candidates were extracted from the second paper of our series work (hereafter, Paper-II) to illustrate their positive role in mitigating contamination from projected quasars and quasar-star projections. We also reviewed and discussed the confirmation strategies for dual and lensed quasar candidates, and outlined future confirmation strategies for them in the context of the era dominated by large-scale spectroscopic and imaging surveys.

AI.tldr: This paper confirms 11 quasar pair candidates from the MGQPC catalog through low-resolution long-slit spectroscopy, discovering 6 dual quasars and 3 projected quasars, including one high-redshift dual quasar (z~3.1). It investigates missed detections by previous surveys, discusses lensing configurations and quasar-star projections, and outlines future confirmation strategies for the era of large-scale surveys.
AI.motivation: To spectroscopically confirm quasar pair candidates selected from the MGQPC catalog, identify genuine dual quasars versus projected pairs, and understand why previous surveys missed these objects, thereby improving selection and confirmation strategies for future large-scale surveys.
AI.method: Low-resolution long-slit spectroscopy using 5 spectrographs on 3 telescopes; photometric redshifts from Paper-II; analysis of lensing configurations and quasar-star projections; comparison with previous survey data to identify missed quasars.
AI.result: Confirmed 6 dual quasars (one at z~3.1) and 3 projected quasars; LQ hypothesis cannot be fully ruled out for 3 dual quasars; identified reasons for previous survey misses; discussed a wide-separation lensing candidate and two quasar-star projections mimicking lensed quasars.
AI.conclusion: Photometric redshifts from Paper-II help mitigate contamination from projected quasars and quasar-star projections. The study reviews current confirmation strategies and outlines improved approaches for the era of large-scale spectroscopic and imaging surveys.

title: Spectroscopic Monitoring of Metal Lines in Polluted White Dwarfs
comment: Accepted for publication in The Astrophysical Journal 21 pages, 7 figures
summary: The disruption and accretion of planetary material onto white dwarfs is expected to be inherently dynamic and stochastic, potentially driving variability in the accretion rate and therefore the shape and depth of the photospheric metal absorption lines. This paper presents an 18-year optical spectroscopic monitoring campaign of five warm (11,000-23,000K) polluted white dwarfs with sinking timescales of days-months, observed using Magellan/MIKE and SALT/HRS to directly test this prediction. At four of the five systems, no statistically significant variability is detected over baselines of 15-18 years corresponding to hundreds to thousands of diffusion timescales, with inferred accretion rates stable to within 15-30% (1$σ$) showing remarkably stable accretion on decadal timescales. This implies that either the processes maintaining the accretion of the disrupted planetary material are stable on the same timescales, or that currently uncharacterized photospheric processes act to smooth observable abundance variations on these timescales. The one exception, WD 0106$-$328, shows statistically significant variability in the 4481A Mg II doublet from the ground-based data. Yet no significant equivalent width or abundance changes are seen between two Hubble Space Telescope ultraviolet spectra taken in 2016 and 2025, despite probing a larger set of transitions. This may imply that the ground-based observations witnessed a stochastic excursion from a stable baseline accretion rate, rather than a sustained change in the bulk accretion rate.

AI.tldr: An 18-year optical spectroscopic monitoring campaign of five warm polluted white dwarfs reveals remarkably stable accretion rates (within 15-30%) at four systems, with only one showing variability in ground-based data—though not confirmed by HST UV spectra—suggesting either stable accretion processes or uncharacterized photospheric smoothing effects.
AI.motivation: The disruption and accretion of planetary material onto white dwarfs is expected to be inherently dynamic and stochastic, potentially driving variability in accretion rate and photospheric metal absorption lines. This study directly tests this prediction.
AI.method: Optical spectroscopic monitoring campaign of five warm (11,000-23,000K) polluted white dwarfs with sinking timescales of days-months over 18 years, using Magellan/MIKE and SALT/HRS, supplemented by HST UV spectra for one target.
AI.result: No statistically significant variability detected at four of five systems over 15-18 years (hundreds to thousands of diffusion timescales), with inferred accretion rates stable to within 15-30% (1σ). WD 0106−328 showed variability in the 4481Å Mg II doublet in ground-based data, but no significant changes between two HST UV spectra taken 9 years apart.
AI.conclusion: Accretion onto polluted white dwarfs is remarkably stable on decadal timescales, implying either stable accretion processes maintaining disrupted planetary material or uncharacterized photospheric processes smoothing observable abundance variations. The single variable case suggests stochastic excursions from a stable baseline rather than sustained accretion rate changes.

title: The Stellar "Snake"-V: the census within 3 kpc in the Solar Neighborhood
comment: 35 pages, 13 figures, 5 tables. Comments and collaboration are welcome. The Snake Serials: https://astrotian.github.io/snake. The visualization: https://astrotian.github.io/snake/visualization
summary: We present a Gaia DR3 source-level census of \emph{Stellar Snake} complexes within 3\,kpc of the Sun. We define a Stellar Snake as a mutually coherent association of two or more stellar overdensities, characterised by consistent positions, kinematics, orbital invariants, ages, and chemical properties, rather than as a single gravitationally bound object. Moving beyond catalogue-driven searches seeded by known open clusters, our framework operates directly on individual Gaia sources to recover extended, low-density substructures and interconnecting stellar bridges. The multi-stage pipeline extracts statistically significant, non-overlapping base nodes, infers homogeneous parameters using a PointNet point-cloud regressor, and links these nodes into large-scale macro-structures across a 9D space spanning positions, tangential velocities, radial velocity, age \(\log t\), and orbital integrals \((E,L_Z)\). After FoF-topology cross-validation and boundary resolution, the final catalogue contains 1,256 Stellar Snake candidates comprising 802,489 unique member-star entries in 5,491 final base nodes selected from a 9,909-node input pool. Derived parameters are validated against external open-cluster catalogues and spectroscopic benchmarks. To quantify structural coherence, we introduce a graph-relation Snake Reliability Index (SRI), coupled with a peripheral-branch diagnostic and Gold/Silver/Bronze quality flags. At the population level, the census shows a broad age--metallicity pattern, a declining upper envelope of member-star entries toward older ages, and a projected association between young Snake nodes, nearby spiral-arm loci, and the Radcliffe Wave. This homogeneous inventory provides an observational foundation for probing the formation, coherence, and dynamical evolution of hierarchical stellar complexes in the Milky Way.

AI.tldr: A Gaia DR3-based census identifies 1,256 Stellar Snake complexes (coherent associations of stellar overdensities) within 3 kpc of the Sun, using a direct source-level pipeline with PointNet regression, 9D parameter linking, and a new Snake Reliability Index (SRI).
AI.motivation: To move beyond catalog-driven searches seeded by known open clusters and directly recover extended, low-density substructures and interconnecting stellar bridges, providing a homogeneous observational foundation for studying hierarchical stellar complexes.
AI.method: Multi-stage pipeline: (1) extract statistically significant, non-overlapping base nodes from individual Gaia sources; (2) infer homogeneous parameters via PointNet point-cloud regressor; (3) link nodes into macro-structures in 9D space (positions, tangential velocities, radial velocity, age log t, orbital integrals E, L_Z); (4) FoF-topology cross-validation and boundary resolution; (5) compute Snake Reliability Index (SRI) and Gold/Silver/Bronze quality flags.
AI.result: 1,256 Stellar Snake candidates, 802,489 unique member-star entries, 5,491 final base nodes selected from 9,909-node input pool. Validated against external open-cluster catalogues and spectroscopic benchmarks. Reveals broad age–metallicity pattern, declining upper envelope of member-star entries toward older ages, and projected association between young Snake nodes, nearby spiral-arm loci, and the Radcliffe Wave.
AI.conclusion: This homogeneous inventory provides an observational foundation for probing formation, coherence, and dynamical evolution of hierarchical stellar complexes in the Milky Way.

title: Stellar masses and ages in Gaia Data Release 4 from the Final Luminosity Age Mass Estimator algorithm
comment: to be accepted upon minor revision by A&A
summary: The masses and ages of stars are key quantities for understanding exoplanetary, stellar, and galactic evolution. In the context of Gaia, these parameters provide insights into the stellar populations, helping to trace the formation and history of the Galaxy. As part of the Gaia Data Processing and Analysis Consortium (DPAC), the Final Luminosity Age Mass Estimator (FLAME) pipeline processes Gaia data to derive stellar parameters comprising luminosities, radii, masses and ages. This paper discusses the methods and data used in FLAME for Gaia Data releases and the expected performances of FLAME for the 4th Gaia Data Release. FLAME comprises two main components: the first one, which is analytical, is used to estimate luminosity, radius, and radial velocity correction due to gravitational redshift by exploiting the atmospheric, astrometric, and photometric parameters produced within Gaia. The second is a model inference based on two main approaches: a classical minimization approach, and a Bayesian framework. It aims to derive mass, age, and evolutionary stage. The two step implementation offers flexibility in handling photometric properties that are prone to systematic errors. Tests with simulated data, the Sun, and well characterised samples of stars show that the methods in FLAME perform as expected, producing results in statistical agreement with the literature. We provide new stellar fundamental parameters for some high velocity stars, stars with very low mass companions, and a selection of stars in the Plato Field of View. In Gaia Data Release 4 approximately 500 million sources will have results from the pipeline. [abridged]

AI.tldr: This paper describes the FLAME pipeline developed by DPAC for Gaia Data Release 4, which uses a two-component approach (analytical estimation of luminosity/radius/gravitational redshift, and model inference via minimization/Bayesian methods) to derive stellar parameters (luminosities, radii, masses, ages, evolutionary stages) for ~500 million sources, validated against simulations, the Sun, and literature samples.
AI.motivation: Stellar masses and ages are fundamental for understanding exoplanetary, stellar, and galactic evolution, and Gaia provides a unique opportunity to derive these parameters at scale for millions of stars.
AI.method: FLAME has two components: (1) an analytical component that estimates luminosity, radius, and gravitational redshift correction using atmospheric, astrometric, and photometric parameters from Gaia; (2) a model inference component using a classical minimization approach and a Bayesian framework to derive mass, age, and evolutionary stage. This two-step design provides flexibility against systematic photometric errors.
AI.result: Tests with simulated data, the Sun, and well-characterized stellar samples show statistical agreement with literature values. The pipeline provides new fundamental parameters for high-velocity stars, stars with very low mass companions, and stars in the Plato Field of View. Gaia DR4 will deliver results for ~500 million sources.
AI.conclusion: The FLAME methods perform as expected and will produce reliable stellar parameters for hundreds of millions of sources in Gaia Data Release 4, contributing significantly to stellar population studies and Galactic archaeology.

title: AGN radiative feedback as the main regulator of [O III] outflow activity and obscuration in X-ray AGN
comment: Accepted for publication in Astronomy and Astrophysics (A&A)
summary: Large-scale ionised outflows and nuclear obscuration are fundamental manifestations of AGN activity, yet direct observational evidence linking these phenomena remains scarce. We use the eROSITA Final Equatorial Depth Survey, among the largest uniform optical spectroscopic datasets of X-ray AGN, to investigate how AGN accretion rate affects ionised outflow kinematics and X-ray obscuration. Our sample comprises 2.840 AGN at z<0.82 with high-quality SDSS spectra. Through optical spectral fitting, we measure Eddington ratios ($λ_{Edd}$) and [O III] emission-line kinematics, tracing ionised outflows. In addition, we use archival eROSITA X-ray spectroscopy with X-ray stacking analyses to constrain the obscuration of the sample, $N_H$. We find that (1) 35% of the entire sample hosts a [O III] outflows ($W_{80}>600$ km/s), with the outflow incidence increasing with the AGN luminosity from 15% at $L_{AGN}<10^{44}$ erg/s up to 60% at $L_{AGN}>10^{46}$ erg/s; (2) the outflow incidence increases with Eddington ratio from 29% at $\log λ_{Edd}<-2.3$ to 50% at $\log λ_{Edd}>-1.7$; and (3) the AGN obscuration decreases with Eddington ratio, as sources with $\logλ_{Edd}>-1.7$ are 5 times less obscured than lower Eddington ratios AGN. In addition, we find that 1% of the sample populates the "forbidden region" of the $N_H-λ_{Edd}$ plane, where the outflow incidence peaks at 52%, consistent with a short-lived feedback phase. Notably, when matching the Eddington ratios samples in AGN luminosity, these trends vanish, implying that radiation pressure drives changes in outflow activity and obscuration, while the black hole mass does not play a significant role. Our results are in agreement with AGN radiative feedback scenarios, where the Eddington ratio regulates the AGN environment by driving powerful, galaxy-wide outflows and shaping the amount of circumnuclear material.

AI.tldr: Using eROSITA and SDSS data from 2,840 AGN at z<0.82, this study finds that 35% host [O III] outflows; outflow incidence increases with AGN luminosity (15%→60%) and Eddington ratio (29%→50%); X-ray obscuration decreases with Eddington ratio; and only 1% occupy the "forbidden region" where outflow incidence peaks at 52%. These trends vanish after matching Eddington ratio samples in luminosity, indicating radiation pressure (not black hole mass) drives outflow activity and obscuration.
AI.motivation: To directly link large-scale ionised outflows and nuclear obscuration as AGN manifestations by investigating how accretion rate affects outflow kinematics and X-ray obscuration, addressing the scarcity of direct observational evidence connecting these phenomena.
AI.method: Sample of 2,840 X-ray AGN at z<0.82 from eROSITA Final Equatorial Depth Survey with SDSS optical spectra. Optical spectral fitting measured Eddington ratios and [O III] kinematics (W80>600 km/s for outflows). eROSITA X-ray spectroscopy with stacking analyses constrained NH. Samples matched in AGN luminosity to test mass vs. radiation effects.
AI.result: (1) 35% host outflows; incidence rises with AGN luminosity (15%→60%). (2) Outflow incidence increases with Eddington ratio (29%→50%). (3) Obscuration decreases with Eddington ratio (5× less obscured at high λEdd). (4) 1% occupy "forbidden region" with 52% outflow peak. Trends vanish after luminosity matching, indicating radiation pressure (not MBH) drives these effects.
AI.conclusion: Results support AGN radiative feedback scenarios where Eddington ratio regulates the AGN environment by driving powerful outflows and shaping circumnuclear material, with radiation pressure as the primary driver rather than black hole mass.

title: White Dwarf Classification of DESI DR1 Spectra1
summary: We present a new catalog of spectroscopically confirmed white dwarfs from the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI) Data Release 1. We visually classified 44,417 white dwarf spectra and derived atmospheric parameters for 29,072 DA white dwarfs through spectroscopic model fitting. The resulting mass distribution is non-Gaussian, with a mean mass of $0.677\,M_\odot$, consistent with previous studies. We identify 547 magnetic white dwarfs by detecting Zeeman splitting, including 84 new discoveries, and estimate their magnetic field strengths using off-centered, inclined dipole models when possible. We compare our magnetic field determinations with previous measurements and find overall good agreement. Finally, we investigate the relation between stellar properties and magnetism, finding that magnetic white dwarfs are systematically more massive than the general white dwarf population and that intermediate-strength magnetic fields are already present in stars that have not yet entered the crystallization phase. This result suggests that crystallization is unlikely to be the sole mechanism responsible for the origin of magnetic fields in white dwarfs.

AI.tldr: A new catalog of 44,417 spectroscopically confirmed white dwarfs from DESI Data Release 1 is presented, with atmospheric parameters derived for 29,072 DA white dwarfs, revealing a mean mass of 0.677 M☉, 547 magnetic white dwarfs (84 new), and evidence that crystallization is not the sole origin of magnetic fields.
AI.motivation: To construct a large, uniform catalog of spectroscopically confirmed white dwarfs from DESI DR1, characterize their atmospheric parameters and mass distribution, identify magnetic white dwarfs, and investigate the origin of magnetic fields in white dwarfs.
AI.method: Visual classification of 44,417 white dwarf spectra; spectroscopic model fitting to derive atmospheric parameters for 29,072 DA white dwarfs; detection of magnetic white dwarfs via Zeeman splitting; magnetic field strength estimation using off-centered, inclined dipole models.
AI.result: Mean mass of 0.677 M☉ with non-Gaussian distribution; 547 magnetic white dwarfs identified (84 new); magnetic white dwarfs are systematically more massive; intermediate-strength magnetic fields exist in pre-crystallization stars.
AI.conclusion: Crystallization is unlikely to be the sole mechanism responsible for the origin of magnetic fields in white dwarfs.

title: SchwarMAX: a GPU-friendly Schwarzschild orbit-superposition modelling framework
comment: 15 pages, 10 figures, 2 appendices. Submitted to MNRAS. Comments are welcome!
summary: The Schwarzschild orbit-superposition method is a highly flexible dynamical modelling tool. It constrains the mass distribution of a galaxy using line-of-sight velocity and photometric observations. However, constructing such a dynamical model of a galaxy is computationally expensive. We present SchwarMAX, a new publicly available GPU implementation of the Schwarzschild orbit-superposition method. The GPU-native code is significantly faster than other implementations, with entire model construction taking around a second on GPU A100. Using SchwarMAX, we can explore the distributions of both baryonic and dark matter in a galaxy across a high-dimensional parameter space. We demonstrate its performance using mock integrated-field spectroscopic unit data generated from an N-body simulated barred galaxy. We explore the 12-dimensional space of disc, bar and halo parameters using Markov Chain Monte Carlo. The density profiles and the bar pattern speed of the galaxy are recovered with good accuracy. We show that the code can be applied to barred galaxies across a wide range of inclination angles and can be easily extended to other stellar systems, such as elliptical and dwarf galaxies.

AI.tldr: SchwarMAX is a new GPU-accelerated implementation of the Schwarzschild orbit-superposition method that constructs dynamical models of galaxies in ~1 second on an A100 GPU, enabling MCMC exploration of a 12-dimensional parameter space (disc, bar, halo) to recover density profiles and bar pattern speed with good accuracy.
AI.motivation: The Schwarzschild orbit-superposition method is computationally expensive, limiting its applicability for exploring high-dimensional parameter spaces of baryonic and dark matter distributions in galaxies.
AI.method: A GPU-native (CUDA) implementation of the Schwarzschild orbit-superposition method, combined with MCMC for parameter exploration; demonstrated on mock IFU data from an N-body simulated barred galaxy.
AI.result: Whole model construction takes ~1 second on GPU A100; density profiles and bar pattern speed recovered accurately across a 12-dimensional parameter space; applicable to barred galaxies at various inclinations.
AI.conclusion: SchwarMAX dramatically accelerates Schwarzschild modelling, enabling high-dimensional Bayesian inference of galaxy mass distributions, and is extensible to elliptical and dwarf galaxies.

title: Optimization Algorithm for Determining the Source Surface Radius Based on Parker Solar Probe in situ Measurements from Encounters 1 to 19
comment: 52 pages,11 figures
summary: The Potential Field Source Surface (PFSS) extrapolation is a method for estimating the large scale coronal magnetic field from photospheric magnetograms. The source surface serves as the outer boundary of its solution domain, and is typically a spherical surface. An appropriate source surface radius ($R_{ss}$) enables more accurate identification of the coronal magnetic field topology and estimation of the open flux, thereby potentially enhancing the accuracy of space weather modeling. We prove the well-posedness of the PFSS forward problem and establish the existence and uniqueness of the optimal source surface by combining compactness of the admissible set with continuity of the objective functional. The objective functional is the mean squared error (MSE) between PFSS extrapolation and Parker Solar Probe (PSP) radial magnetic field measurements after Parker spiral backmapping and radial scaling for Encounters 1-19. The optimization algorithm is validated with an analytical solution, and Advanced Composition Explorer (ACE) in situ measurements are used as an independent cross-validation dataset. Additional evaluation metrics and Pareto analysis are used to identify the dominant metrics between open flux and polarity prediction accuracy. Our results show that the optimal $R_{ss}$ derived from the algorithm generally increase from solar minimum into the ascending phase of solar cycle 25. The optimized solution improves open flux agreement while preserving or improving polarity prediction accuracy relative to $2.5R_{s}$. The Pareto frontiers show a transition for dominant metrics from open flux during solar minimum to polarity prediction accuracy during the ascending phase.

AI.tldr: This paper proves the well-posedness of the PFSS forward problem and develops an optimization algorithm to determine the optimal source surface radius ($R_{ss}$) by minimizing MSE against PSP radial magnetic field measurements. The optimal $R_{ss}$ increases from solar minimum to the ascending phase of solar cycle 25, improving open flux agreement while preserving polarity prediction accuracy. Pareto analysis reveals a transition in dominant metrics from open flux (solar minimum) to polarity accuracy (ascending phase).
AI.motivation: The source surface radius ($R_{ss}$) in PFSS extrapolation significantly affects the accuracy of coronal magnetic field topology and open flux estimation, which impacts space weather modeling. The paper aims to determine the optimal $R_{ss}$ in a mathematically rigorous manner.
AI.method: Well-posedness of the PFSS forward problem is proved using compactness of the admissible set and continuity of the objective functional. The objective functional is MSE between PFSS extrapolation and PSP radial magnetic field measurements (Encounters 1-19) after Parker spiral backmapping and radial scaling. The optimization algorithm is validated with an analytical solution and cross-validated with ACE in situ measurements. Pareto analysis identifies dominant metrics between open flux and polarity prediction accuracy.
AI.result: Optimal $R_{ss}$ increases from solar minimum to the ascending phase of solar cycle 25. The optimized solution improves open flux agreement while preserving or improving polarity prediction accuracy relative to the standard $2.5R_{s}$. Pareto frontiers show a transition: open flux dominates during solar minimum, polarity prediction accuracy dominates during the ascending phase.
AI.conclusion: The mathematically rigorous optimization approach successfully determines the time-varying optimal source surface radius, enhancing PFSS-based space weather modeling capabilities.

title: Far-infrared observations of dust in Ly$α$ emitters at z=2-6
summary: The bright Ly$α$ line is regularly used to identify high-redshift star-forming galaxies known as Ly$α$ emitters (LAEs). However, Ly$α$ is affected by resonant scattering and dust absorption making interpretation of its brightness challenging without additional observations. We use SCUBA-2, PACS and SPIRE data to investigate the far-infrared emission, Ly$α$ escape fraction ($f{esc}$(Ly$α$)) and infrared excess (IRX=LIR/LUV) in $\sim$4000 LAEs at z=2.2-6 from SC4K. Five LAEs, all hosting AGN, are individually detected with fluxes $S_{850}$ = 3.7-5.5 mJy at 850$μ\mathrm{m}$. Stacking is used to probe the average emission from all individually undetected LAEs, though the stacks are undetected at all wavelengths (e.g. $S_{850}$ < 0.09 mJy; 3$σ$). We group the sample into bins of redshift, stellar mass, Ly$α$ luminosity and AGN status. Most subsets are undetected but LAEs containing AGN and that have high stellar masses ($M_{\star} = 10^{10} - 10^{12}\, M_{\odot}$; including and excluding AGN) are detected at most wavelengths, suggesting that stellar mass and AGN heating may be enhancing the dust visibility. Individually detected LAEs and detected stacks have $f{esc}$(Ly$α$)=1-7%, while all undetected stacks $\geq$ 10%. All LAEs together average over > 21% and display significant scatter, suggesting a clumpy ISM dust distribution. Non-zero $f{esc}$(Ly$α$) in massive and AGN-hosting LAEs suggests ionizing photons may escape even from dusty galaxies, challenging the idea that dusty galaxies are poor leakers. Examination of the IRX-$β_{UV}$ relation shows LAEs have higher IRX than typical star-forming galaxies at similar redshifts. However, our detections tend to favour more massive, AGN-hosting systems and deeper observations are therefore needed.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes ~4000 LAEs at z=2.2-6 from SC4K using SCUBA-2, PACS, and SPIRE data. Only five AGN-hosting LAEs are individually detected at 850μm. Stacking shows most undetected LAEs have weak far-IR emission. Detected sources have Lyα escape fractions of 1-7%, while undetected stacks have ≥10%. LAEs show higher IRX than typical star-forming galaxies, and non-zero escape fractions in dusty/AGN hosts challenge the assumption that dusty galaxies are poor Lyα leakers.
AI.motivation: To understand the relationship between Lyα emission, dust content, and escape fraction in high-redshift LAEs, and to investigate whether dusty or AGN-hosting galaxies can still leak Lyα and ionizing photons.
AI.method: Far-IR observations with SCUBA-2 (850μm), PACS, and SPIRE combined with stacking analysis on ~4000 LAEs from SC4K, grouped by redshift, stellar mass, Lyα luminosity, and AGN status.
AI.result: Only 5 AGN-hosting LAEs individually detected; most stacks undetected (S850<0.09 mJy). AGN and high-mass stacks detected. Detected sources have fesc(Lyα)=1-7%; undetected stacks ≥10%; all LAEs average >21% with large scatter. LAEs show higher IRX than typical SFGs.
AI.conclusion: Non-zero Lyα escape fractions in massive and AGN-hosting dusty LAEs challenge the view that dusty galaxies are poor leakers. Clumpy ISM dust distribution may explain the scatter. Deeper observations are needed to confirm trends.

title: SPHEREx 0.75 to 5 $μ$m Spectra for a Sequence of Nearby Brown Dwarfs
comment: 27 pages, 20 figures
summary: The SPHEREx all-sky survey has now measured the R$\sim$40-100 infrared spectra of thousands of nearby brown dwarfs in the chemically rich 0.75-5 $μ$m range. The survey's wide spectral coverage and high S/N permits flux measurements that capture several broadband molecular absorption features, and upwards of 80$\%$ of the total bolometric luminosity of most brown dwarfs. Atmospheric models are known to yield systematic disagreements in the inferred temperatures and radii of brown dwarfs, necessitating benchmarking against observations. In this work, we present SPHEREx spectra across a broad sequence of 37 nearby field brown dwarfs, ranging from L0 to Y4 ($\sim$2500-250 K) and compare them to theoretical expectations. We additionally compile spectra for separate low-gravity and low-metallicity objects, and show how they trend with constant spectral type. We fit the measured spectra to the well-known forward model grids Sonora Diamondback, Elf Owl, BT-Settl, ATMO2020 and ATMO2020++ and compare their goodness-of-fit as a function of wavelength, spectral type, and treatment of clouds and chemistry. We find that the models continue to struggle to simultaneously fit the J/H/K peaks and the 4 $μ$m opacity window, especially in L/T transition objects. The largest deviations appear around the chemistry-sensitive CO$_2$ and CO features. Despite these offsets, the models broadly capture their trends across the L/T transition, with the observed sample of field dwarfs strongly preferring the weak vertical mixing ($k_\mathrm{zz}$ = 10$^4$ cm$^2$s$^{-1}$) Elf Owl models over strong mixing. The spectra shown here along with future SPHEREx data will help guide improvements to models.

AI.tldr: SPHEREx spectra of 37 nearby brown dwarfs (L0–Y4) are compared to five atmospheric models, finding systematic mismatches in J/H/K peaks and CO₂/CO features, with best fits from weak vertical mixing (Elf Owl) models.
AI.motivation: Atmospheric models yield systematic disagreements in inferred temperatures and radii of brown dwarfs, so benchmarking against high-quality observed spectra is needed to improve theoretical predictions.
AI.method: SPHEREx all-sky survey provides R~40-100 infrared spectra (0.75–5 μm) of 37 brown dwarfs (L0–Y4, ~2500–250 K), plus low-gravity and low-metallicity objects. Observed spectra are fit to five forward model grids: Sonora Diamondback, Elf Owl, BT-Settl, ATMO2020, and ATMO2020++, assessing goodness-of-fit across wavelength, spectral type, clouds, and chemistry.
AI.result: Models struggle to simultaneously fit J/H/K peaks and the 4 μm opacity window, especially in L/T transition objects; largest deviations occur at CO₂ and CO features. Field dwarfs strongly prefer weak vertical mixing (k_zz = 10⁴ cm²s⁻¹) Elf Owl models over strong mixing.
AI.conclusion: Despite systematic offsets, models broadly capture trends across the L/T transition. SPHEREx data will guide further improvements to brown dwarf atmospheric models.

title: How can we finally see the first light? Status and perspective in the search for Population III stars
comment: 27 pages, 14 figures, 3 tables. Proceeding of "The search for Pop III stars" session of the CSI: Sesto workshop, January 26-30 2026. Submitted to the Open Journal of Astrophysics
summary: Finding the first (Population III or Pop III) stars is one of the fundamental quests of astronomy, aiming to deliver the missing link in how stars form at early cosmic times. Yet their initial mass function, formation sites and feedback remain highly uncertain, as well as the timing and topology of the transition to metal-enriched star formation. The observability of their peculiar spectral features is also debated, due to their short lifetime and faintness. This review summarizes current theoretical expectations for Pop III star formation, and the main observational strategies that have been adopted to constrain their properties across cosmic time, including near-field cosmology studies, direct searches for extremely metal-poor star-forming complexes and/or hard-ionizing spectral signatures at high and intermediate redshifts, and prospects for identifying Pop III activity up to Cosmic Dawn. The combination of JWST spectroscopy, time-domain searches, lensing surveys, stellar archaeology, absorption-line studies, as well as improved simulations, is yielding a growing number of observational candidates and narrowing the allowed parameter space for the first stars, setting the stage for a ``golden era'' of Pop III searches.

AI.tldr: This review summarizes theoretical expectations for Pop III star formation and observational strategies to detect them, including JWST spectroscopy, lensing, stellar archaeology, and simulations, setting the stage for a "golden era" of Pop III searches.
AI.motivation: Finding the first (Population III) stars is a fundamental quest to understand star formation at early cosmic times, but their properties (IMF, feedback, formation sites) and observability remain highly uncertain.
AI.method: The paper reviews theoretical models of Pop III star formation and synthesizes observational strategies: near-field cosmology, direct searches for extremely metal-poor star-forming complexes, hard-ionizing spectral signatures at high/intermediate redshifts, and prospects for identifying Pop III activity up to Cosmic Dawn.
AI.result: Combining JWST spectroscopy, time-domain surveys, lensing, stellar archaeology, absorption-line studies, and improved simulations is yielding growing observational candidates and narrowing the allowed parameter space for the first stars.
AI.conclusion: The current multi-pronged observational and theoretical effort is setting the stage for a "golden era" of Pop III star searches, with emerging candidates and tighter constraints on first star properties.

title: Constraining the model-based uncertainties of asteroseismic magnetic field measurements in red giants
comment: 14 pages, 12 figures, 1 table, submitted to A&A, abstract condensed to meet arXiv requirements
summary: Magnetic fields inside red giants are measured using shifts to the oscillation frequencies. However, in the asymptotic framework, converting a frequency shift into a radial magnetic field strength requires knowing the global magnetic sensitivity. This parameter (also called the core structure parameter) must be inferred from stellar models, introducing a source of uncertainty. We seek to understand how the global magnetic sensitivity depends on stellar properties such as mass and metallicity, and to quantify the model-based uncertainty on magnetic field measurements. We also explore which stellar properties are key to finding a precise and accurate estimate of the global magnetic sensitivity. Using MESA models, we examine how the global magnetic sensitivity changes with mass, metallicity, and age. We then create a set of synthetic stars and test how well we recover the sensitivity parameter. We consider different grid construction approaches and the choice of which observables are used in the fitting process. We find that the global magnetic sensitivity shows a stronger dependence on mass for higher mass models and a stronger metallicity dependence for lower metallicity models. Our approach recovers the sensitivity parameter well, with an uncertainty of 10% when precise metallicity measurements are used. We apply our method to stars with existing magnetic field measurements. In most cases, the dominant source of uncertainty remains observational, although precise modeling can significantly reduce the magnetic field uncertainty for stars with exceptional data. With careful fitting, models yield accurate values for the global magnetic sensitivity. We recommend that future work obtain the global magnetic sensitivity using both asteroseismic and high-quality spectroscopic data. Under these conditions, we recommend adopting a model-based uncertainty of 10% on the sensitivity parameter.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates how the global magnetic sensitivity parameter — needed to infer red giant magnetic fields from oscillation frequency shifts — depends on stellar mass, metallicity, and age, and quantifies model-based uncertainties. Using MESA models, the authors find sensitivity depends more strongly on mass for higher-mass stars and on metallicity for lower-metallicity stars. They recover the parameter with ~10% uncertainty when precise metallicity is available, and recommend a 10% model-based uncertainty for future work using combined asteroseismic and spectroscopic data.
AI.motivation: To understand the dependence of the global magnetic sensitivity on stellar properties (mass, metallicity, age) and to quantify model-based uncertainty in magnetic field measurements of red giants, which currently relies on an uncertain model-dependent parameter.
AI.method: MESA stellar models were used to examine how global magnetic sensitivity varies with mass, metallicity, and age. Synthetic stars were generated and tested for recovery of the sensitivity parameter under different grid construction approaches and choices of observables.
AI.result: Global magnetic sensitivity shows stronger mass dependence for higher-mass models and stronger metallicity dependence for lower-metallicity models. The parameter is recovered with ~10% uncertainty when precise metallicity measurements are used. For most stars with existing measurements, observational uncertainty dominates, but precise modeling helps for stars with exceptional data.
AI.conclusion: Future work should obtain global magnetic sensitivity using both asteroseismic and high-quality spectroscopic data, adopting a model-based uncertainty of 10% on the sensitivity parameter.

title: The evolution of high-z proto-star clusters into local globular clusters
comment: 6 pages, 3 figures, accepted for publication by A&A Letters
summary: The James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) detected numerous massive and relatively compact stellar clumps around proto-galaxies at high redshift (z>0.5). Their properties suggest that these systems may represent proto-globular clusters (GCs), but their possible connection to local old GCs is poorly understood. In this Letter, we explore the dynamical evolution of proto-star clusters, building the missing evolutionary link between high-z systems observed by JWST and local GCs. Our simulations include the effects of stellar interactions, stellar evolution, and the strong time-dependent cosmological tidal field in which these proto-star clusters evolve. We also explore the role of multiple stellar populations and stellar-mass black holes (BHs), two fundamental ingredients in stellar cluster dynamics. We show that systems hosting multiple populations (as routinely observed in local GCs) are more likely to endure the early strong tidal field than single-population clusters. In addition, after 12 Gyr, such systems have properties consistent with those of Galactic GCs. Our work confirms that the high-z clumps observed by JWST can be the progenitors of the local GCs. Finally, we show that a population of stellar-mass BHs within a proto-star cluster favors its disruption, but that surviving systems can retain a sizable population of BHs.

AI.tldr: This paper demonstrates that the massive stellar clumps observed by JWST at high redshift can evolve into local globular clusters (GCs), with multiple stellar populations aiding survival through early strong tidal fields, while stellar-mass black holes promote cluster disruption.
AI.motivation: JWST has detected massive compact stellar clumps around high-redshift (z>0.5) proto-galaxies that resemble proto-globular clusters, but whether these systems are indeed the progenitors of old local GCs remains unclear, motivating a dynamical evolution study to bridge this gap.
AI.method: The authors performed simulations of proto-star cluster dynamical evolution incorporating stellar interactions, stellar evolution, and time-dependent cosmological tidal fields, while also examining the effects of multiple stellar populations and stellar-mass black holes.
AI.result: Systems with multiple stellar populations survive early strong tidal fields better than single-population clusters and, after 12 Gyr, match Galactic GC properties. Stellar-mass BHs promote cluster disruption, but surviving systems retain a sizable BH population.
AI.conclusion: The high-z clumps detected by JWST are indeed viable progenitors of local GCs, confirming the evolutionary link between these early-universe structures and present-day globular clusters.

title: Unravelling the nonthermal emissions from the quiet solar corona with the SKA
comment: Published in Advancing Astrophysics with the SKA II (AASKAII), 2026 (arXiv:2606.20366). Report-no:AASKAII/Mondal01 . Advancing Astrophysics with the SKA II (AASKAII) outlines the transformative scientific advances that will be enabled by the SKA telescopes
summary: Investigation of the nonthermal emissions from the quiet solar corona has been rather limited. This primarily stems from the fact that the emission is expected to be quite weak and very high dynamic range images are required to detect such emissions. Although, the few detections of the nonthermal emissions have all come from the radio band, the past observations had several issues, the most important being the low image fidelity and lack of simultaneous broadband observation capability. Recent observations have been able to tackle many of these prior difficulties using modern instrumentation, and have produced multiple interesting results. In spite of these improvements, multiple challenges remain. For example, most of the recent investigations were only able to focus on the brightest of these events, due to rather poor spectroscopic snapshot PSF of the instruments. The SKA, with its excellent sensitivity as well as its exquisite spectroscopic snapshot PSF would be a game-changer in this field. It would not only allow us to detect and characterise these emissions in Stokes I, but would also allow us to investigate their polarisation properties as well. The high angular resolution offered by the SKA will allow a unique association of the detected radio transients with their thermal counterparts. This would enable us to investigate the thermal-nonthermal energy partition even for these rather weak transient emissions, which in turn would allow validation of particle acceleration and magnetic reconnection theories in a regime vastly different from that done previously. In addition, characterization of the nonthermal emissions of these weak coronal transients may also provide a new probe to understand how energy is transferred from the photosphere and dumped into the corona, and thus serve as a new tool to tackle the coronal heating problem.

AI.tldr: This paper reviews past limitations and recent progress in detecting nonthermal emissions from the quiet solar corona, and discusses how the Square Kilometre Array (SKA) will be a transformative instrument for detecting, characterizing, and understanding these weak coronal transients and their implications for coronal heating and particle acceleration.
AI.motivation: Investigation of nonthermal emissions from the quiet solar corona has been very limited due to weak signals requiring high dynamic range images, and past observations suffered from low image fidelity and lack of simultaneous broadband capability. Understanding these emissions is crucial for probing energy transfer from the photosphere to the corona and addressing the coronal heating problem.
AI.method: The paper reviews past observational challenges (low fidelity, poor spectroscopic snapshot PSF) and highlights recent improvements using modern instrumentation. It then proposes that the SKA, with its excellent sensitivity, exquisite spectroscopic snapshot PSF, and high angular resolution, will enable detection in Stokes I and polarization, and allow unique association of radio transients with thermal counterparts.
AI.result: Recent modern observations have tackled many prior difficulties and produced multiple interesting results, though most still only focus on the brightest events due to poor spectroscopic snapshot PSF. The SKA is positioned as a game-changer that would enable detection and characterization of weak nonthermal emissions and their polarization properties.
AI.conclusion: The SKA will allow investigation of thermal-nonthermal energy partition for weak transient emissions, enabling validation of particle acceleration and magnetic reconnection theories in a new regime. Characterization of these emissions may also provide a new probe for understanding energy transfer from the photosphere to the corona, contributing to solving the coronal heating problem.

title: Precision near-IR spectroscopy for understanding AGN physics and shed light on the H0 tension -- SHARP Science Book
comment: Accepted for publication in the New Astronomy Special issue SHARP Science Book
summary: The persistent tension between early- and late-Universe measurements of the Hubble constant (H0) remains on of the most significant challenges in modern cosmology. The Spectroastrometry and Reverberation Mapping (SARM) method offers a promising, calibration-independent approach to address this issue by combining time-delay measurements of the Broad-Line Region (BLR) with interferometric angular size determinations. Current implementations of SARM, however, are limited by the difficulty of performing near-infrared reverberation mapping (RM) on the same emission lines observed by GRAVITY, restricting applications to only a few bright AGN. We propose using the capabilities of SHARP, the next-generation near-infrared spectrograph for the Extremely Large Telescope (ELT), to overcome these limitations. SHARP's sensitivity and multi-object spectroscopy will enable (1) efficient long-term monitoring of existing GRAVITY targets with minimal time investment, and (2) systematic RM campaigns for the fainter AGN that will be observed by GRAVITY+. These advances will give us precise infrared lags for tens of AGN, enabling geometric distance measurements and a robust, calibration-free determination of H0. Beyond cosmology, SHARP will allow detailed studies of BLR structure and kinematics in the infrared, advancing our understanding of AGN physics and with repercussion on the measurements of Supermassive Black Holes (SMBH) masses.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes using SHARP, a next-generation near-infrared spectrograph for the ELT, to overcome limitations in the Spectroastrometry and Reverberation Mapping (SARM) method for measuring the Hubble constant (H0). SHARP will enable efficient monitoring of AGN for reverberation mapping, providing precise infrared lags for tens of AGN, enabling calibration-free geometric distance measurements and robust H0 determination, while also advancing AGN physics and SMBH mass studies.
AI.motivation: The persistent tension between early- and late-Universe measurements of H0 remains a major challenge in cosmology. Current SARM implementations are limited by the difficulty of performing near-infrared RM on the same emission lines observed by GRAVITY, restricting applications to only a few bright AGN.
AI.method: The SARM method combines time-delay measurements of the BLR with interferometric angular size determinations. The authors propose using SHARP on the ELT to overcome current limitations through (1) efficient long-term monitoring of existing GRAVITY targets, and (2) systematic RM campaigns for fainter AGN observable by GRAVITY+.
AI.result: SHARP's sensitivity and multi-object spectroscopy will enable precise infrared lags for tens of AGN, enabling geometric distance measurements and robust, calibration-free determination of H0.
AI.conclusion: SHARP will enable calibration-independent H0 measurements to address the Hubble tension, and will also advance AGN physics by enabling detailed studies of BLR structure and kinematics in the infrared, with implications for SMBH mass measurements.

title: Automatic detection of solar filament oscillations I: Multi-scale spectral pipeline
summary:
Solar filament oscillations provide important diagnostics of prominence magnetic structure and stability, but their detection in long Hαarchives has traditionally relied on visual inspection, manually placed slits, and time--distance diagrams. We present an automatic pipeline for detecting spatially coherent filament oscillations in GONG Hαimage sequences. The method combines image preprocessing and coalignment, deep-learning-based filament detection and segmentation, multi-scale spatial averaging, Lomb--Scargle spectral analysis, convolutional-neural-network background estimation, empirical calibration of significance thresholds, and clustering of candidate detections in period and space. Only oscillations supported across at least four spatial scales are retained, reducing sensitivity to local pixel-scale intensity fluctuations.
  The pipeline recovers several events from the manual GONG catalog of Luna et al. (2018), including the 1 January 2014 oscillation with a period of approximately 76 min. Applied to the first two weeks of January 2014, it identifies 91 oscillatory events, compared with 22 non-duplicate events in the corresponding manual catalog, with detected periods ranging from about 20 to 126 min. It also detects previously unreported oscillations, including an event on 13 January 2014 with a period of approximately 86 min that is independently confirmed using a conventional time--distance diagram.
  These results demonstrate that automated filament segmentation, multi-scale spectral analysis, and calibrated significance testing can provide a reproducible and scalable alternative to manual slit-based searches. The pipeline substantially increases detection sensitivity while preferentially selecting coherent filament-scale oscillations, enabling future statistical studies over extended GONG intervals and across the solar cycle.

AI.tldr: An automated pipeline using deep learning, multi-scale spectral analysis, and significance testing detects coherent solar filament oscillations in GONG Hα images, outperforming manual methods in sensitivity and reproducibility.
AI.motivation: Solar filament oscillations are important for diagnosing prominence magnetic structure and stability, but traditional detection relies on manual visual inspection, which is labor-intensive, non-reproducible, and not scalable to large archives.
AI.method: The pipeline integrates: (1) image preprocessing and coalignment, (2) deep-learning-based filament detection and segmentation, (3) multi-scale spatial averaging, (4) Lomb–Scargle spectral analysis, (5) CNN-based background estimation, (6) empirical calibration of significance thresholds, and (7) clustering of candidate detections. Oscillations must be coherent across at least four spatial scales to be retained.
AI.result: Recovered known events (e.g., 76-min oscillation on 1 Jan 2014). Over two weeks, detected 91 oscillatory events vs. 22 non-duplicate manual events, with periods ranging 20–126 min. Discovered previously unreported events (e.g., 86-min oscillation on 13 Jan 2014 confirmed via time–distance diagram).
AI.conclusion: Automated filament segmentation, multi-scale spectral analysis, and calibrated significance testing offer a reproducible, scalable alternative to manual slit-based searches, substantially increasing detection sensitivity while selecting coherent filament-scale oscillations, enabling large-scale statistical studies across the solar cycle.

title: OCCAM X. Neutron Capture Abundances with Keck/HIRES & Magellan/MIKE
summary: The chemistry of stars provides powerful insight into the history of the Milky Way. With multiple large-sky spectroscopic surveys that are currently available, using chemistry as a means to study the evolution and history of the Milky Way has flourished. Open clusters have long been used as landmarks to calibrate different age dating methods (e.g., gyrochronology and asteroseismology). In this work, we utilize the SDSS-IV/APOGEE-based Open Cluster Chemical Abundances and Mapping (OCCAM) survey as our foundation for new optical observations; enabling us to characterize neutron-capture abundances for known cluster members. For 56 stars in 18 open clusters, we collected high-resolution (R > 50,000), high-S/N (>75 at 5500A), spectra from Keck I and Magellan Baade telescopes. With these data, we derive abundances for 23 elements using BACCHUS, including 7 neutron capture abundances not measurable by APOGEE. Finally, we characterize the radial distribution of these neutron-capture elements in the Milky Way. We find that the second-peak s-process and r-process abundances exhibit relatively flat gradients in the Milky Way. Although not as distinct, the first-peak s-process abundances also have slopes which are shallower than the alpha and iron-peak elements. The differences in the neutron-capture gradients from the lighter elements not just indicates the sources producing these elements are fundamentally different, but that the timescales on which they are produced also differ (especially for the r-process). Moreover, a metallicity dependence of the AGB stars responsible for producing the heaviest s-process abundances may be necessary to consider in Galactic evolution models.

AI.tldr: Using high-resolution optical spectra of 56 stars in 18 open clusters, this study derives abundances for 23 elements (including 7 neutron-capture elements not available from APOGEE) and characterizes the radial distribution of neutron-capture elements in the Milky Way, finding flat gradients for second-peak s-process and r-process abundances and shallower slopes for first-peak s-process abundances compared to alpha and iron-peak elements.
AI.motivation: To extend chemical abundance studies of open clusters beyond APOGEE's capabilities by measuring neutron-capture elements, thereby providing better constraints on the nucleosynthetic sources and production timescales of these elements and improving Galactic chemical evolution models.
AI.method: (1) Used the SDSS-IV/APOGEE-based OCCAM survey as a foundation; (2) Collected high-resolution (R>50,000), high-S/N (>75 at 5500Å) spectra from Keck I and Magellan Baade telescopes for 56 stars in 18 open clusters; (3) Derived abundances for 23 elements using the BACCHUS code, including 7 neutron-capture elements not measurable by APOGEE; (4) Characterized the radial distribution of neutron-capture elements in the Milky Way.
AI.result: Second-peak s-process and r-process abundances show relatively flat gradients in the Milky Way. First-peak s-process abundances exhibit shallower slopes than alpha and iron-peak elements. The differences in neutron-capture gradients from lighter elements indicate fundamentally different production sources and timescales, especially for the r-process.
AI.conclusion: The distinct radial gradients of neutron-capture elements compared to lighter elements reveal that their nucleosynthetic sources and production timescales are fundamentally different. A metallicity dependence of AGB stars producing the heaviest s-process abundances may be necessary for accurate Galactic evolution models.

title: Stellar Forcing of (exo)Planetary Environments
comment: 132 Pages, 47 Figures, 8 Tables, Submitted to Space Science Reviews
summary:
The environments of exoplanets are fundamentally shaped by the magnetic activity of their host stars through a combination of radiative, plasma, and particle-driven processes. This article presents a comprehensive overview of the four principal forms of stellar forcing that regulate atmospheric structure, chemistry, escape, and long-term planetary evolution: high-energy radiation, magnetized stellar winds, coronal mass ejections, and energetic particles. Using the Sun as a physically resolved benchmark, the discussion extends toward increasingly active cool stars to establish a broader picture for star--planet interactions across the main sequence.
  The article first examines the production of stellar X-ray and extreme ultraviolet emission from chromospheres and coronae, together with the variability introduced by flares and, more generally, magnetic reconnection processes. Particular attention is given to spectroscopic diagnostics, activity scalings with stellar rotation and age, flare energetics, statistical flare behavior, and the observational connections between impulsive and gradual phases of magnetic energy release. The treatment then shifts to the continuous outflow of magnetized plasma, describing the thermodynamic and magnetic mechanisms that drive stellar winds and the role of multidimensional magnetohydrodynamic modeling in determining wind structure, angular momentum loss, and planetary interaction regimes. Solar and stellar coronal mass ejections are subsequently explored through their observational diagnostics, flare associations, propagation properties, and possible suppression by strong stellar magnetic fields. Finally, the transport and modulation of galactic and stellar energetic particles are discussed, together with current approaches for estimating particle environments in active planetary systems and their consequences for atmospheric chemistry and climate. The article concludes by outlining future observational and numerical developments required to connect these coupled stellar forcing processes within a unified exoplanetary framework.

AI.tldr: This paper reviews how stellar magnetic activity (high-energy radiation, magnetized winds, coronal mass ejections, and energetic particles) shapes exoplanetary atmospheres and evolution, using the Sun as a benchmark and extending to more active cool stars.
AI.motivation: To provide a comprehensive framework connecting the four principal stellar forcing mechanisms that collectively regulate exoplanet atmospheric structure, chemistry, escape, and long-term evolution, bridging solar and stellar observations.
AI.method: A literature review approach: using the Sun as a physically resolved benchmark, extending observational and modeling results (e.g., MHD simulations, spectroscopic diagnostics, flare statistics) to increasingly active cool main-sequence stars.
AI.result: The review maps stellar X-ray/EUV production, flare variability, wind thermodynamics and MHD modeling, CME diagnostics and magnetic suppression, and energetic particle transport across stellar activity levels, identifying key observational links and gaps.
AI.conclusion: Future progress requires unified observational and numerical efforts to couple all stellar forcing processes into a coherent exoplanetary framework, enabling predictive understanding of atmospheric evolution under stellar activity.

title: Probing the Parsec-Scale Dynamical Structure of Ionized Gas in Radio-Quiet AGN with SKA
comment: Published in Advancing Astrophysics with the SKA II (AASKAII), 2026 (arXiv:2606.20366). Report-no:AASKAII/Kudoh01
summary: We systematically organize the radio-emitting components in radio-quiet active galactic nuclei (RQ AGN), including jets, accretion disk coronae, dust, ionized gas outflows, and circumnuclear star formation. We present a diagnostic framework for distinguishing these components using spectral turnovers and spectral indices produced by synchrotron self-absorption (SSA) and free-free absorption (FFA), together with brightness temperature and peak frequency. The central premise is that the observed spectral index and its spatial distribution are not unique source properties unless the observing beam is specified: changing the angular resolution changes the physical scale being sampled and therefore changes the mixture of radio-emitting components. By exploiting this scale dependence with SKA1-MID and SKA-VLBI, spatially resolved spectral-index mapping will reveal which physical processes dominate from circumnuclear star formation on $\sim$100 pc scales to jets, coronal emission, and compact ionized gas on parsec and sub-parsec scales. Through multi-frequency continuum imaging and spectral-index mapping, SKA observations will provide a multi-scale physical view of radio-quiet AGN that links radio emission mechanisms to accretion, obscuration, and feedback.

SKA1-MID and SKA-VLBI multi-frequency imaging will enable spatially resolved spectral-index mapping from ~100 pc to sub-parsec scales to link radio emission to accretion, obscuration, and feedback.

AI.method: A diagnostic framework using spectral turnovers from synchrotron self-absorption (SSA) and free-free absorption (FFA), spectral indices, brightness temperature, and peak frequency. The approach will be applied using SKA1-MID and SKA-VLBI multi-frequency continuum imaging and spectral-index mapping.
